title: How Much Fluid, How Low a Pressure: Undifferentiated Shock Resuscitation Pearls — 2026-08-31
rationale: This episode is built around a genuine, current fault line rather than a manufactured one: the March-2026 Surviving Sepsis Campaign guidelines (30 mL/kg as a floor, a new 60-65 mmHg permissive-hypotension band for over-65s, peripheral vasopressor starts, fluid-then-pressor sequencing) sit in direct operational tension with the UK's own NICE NG253 rewrite, which mandates small titrated 250 mL boluses with senior review rather than a bundle target -- the same "how much fluid" question that ARISE-FLUIDS (St Emlyn's) and the ANDROMEDA-SHOCK-2 capillary-refill-vs-lactate trial (EMCrit) attack from two more angles, and that EMCrit's own cross-examination of the SSC 2026 lead author shows is contested even among the guideline's authors. Because every one of the five verified sources stakes out a citable, non-strawman position on live, currently-unresolved practice questions (fluid volume philosophy, permissive hypotension in the elderly, resuscitation endpoint), this is upgraded from the requested default deep-dive to a debate: the hosts have real, sourced disagreements to argue -- international bundle vs UK titration, capillary refill vs lactate -- not just a guideline to summarize. The mix of one international authority guideline, one UK authority guideline, and three community/FOAMed critiques gives the debate both an institutional anchor and sharp, practising-clinician pushback, which is exactly the tension a UK EM doctor navigates on shift.
case_vignette: A 68-year-old care-home resident is wheeled into resus with urosepsis: BP 78/40, lactate 4.2 mmol/L, and cool, mottled skin to the knees. The FY2 reaches for a 30 mL/kg crystalloid bolus out of habit -- but NICE NG253 says stop and reassess after 250 mL, the fresh SSC 2026 guidance suggests a 65 mmHg MAP target might be too tight for a patient this age, and the consultant on shift wants to titrate off capillary refill time rather than wait for the next lactate. Fluid, pressor, both, and guided by which number -- the room can't agree, and neither can the guidelines.

sources.title: Surviving Sepsis Campaign: International Guidelines for Management of Sepsis and Septic Shock 2026 (SCCM/ESICM)
sources.why: The freshest global anchor (March 2026): 46 new statements bring a strong 65 mmHg MAP target, a NEW 60-65 mmHg permissive-hypotension band for patients ≥65y, peripheral-first vasopressor starts, and 'fluid bolus, then vasopressor if hypotension persists' as the default sequencing -- the framework the rest of the episode's sources push against.

sources.title: NICE NG253: Suspected sepsis in people aged 16 or over — recognition, assessment and early management (fluid resuscitation recommendations updated 2025)
sources.why: The UK's own 2025 rewrite drops the 30 mL/kg bundle target for titrated 250 mL boluses (reassess each time, senior review at 1000 mL) -- a materially different bedside protocol from SSC's international default, and the one this listener is actually mandated to follow.

sources.title: To squeeze or not to squeeze: the ARISE-FLUIDS trial (St Emlyn's)
sources.why: UK-voiced critical appraisal of the ARISE-FLUIDS RCT on restrictive vs liberal fluid volumes in septic shock -- stress-tests SSC's fluid-first sequencing against a fresh 2026 trial read, limitations included.

sources.title: EMCrit 411 - You Need to Understand the Andromeda-Shock-2 RCT for Septic Shock
sources.why: Weingart's deep dive on capillary-refill-time-guided vs lactate-clearance-guided resuscitation targets in the 1,467-patient ANDROMEDA-SHOCK-2 RCT (win ratio 1.16, p=0.04) -- the central 'how do you know you're done resuscitating' fight.

sources.title: EMCrit 422 - SSC 2026 Sepsis Guidelines: The good, the Bad, and the UGLY -- discussion with lead author
sources.why: Weingart interrogates SSC 2026 lead author Hallie Prescott directly on antibiotic timing, fluid volume, and evidence-quality gaps -- turns the anchor guideline itself into a live argument instead of settled doctrine.
